title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text: ggplot2 is based on the grammar of graphics — the idea that you can build every graph from the same components: a data set, a coordinate system, and geoms, visual marks that represent data points.

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
The template
Every ggplot2 chart follows the same basic recipe. Only data, the geom function, and its mapping are required — everything else falls back to sensible defaults.
ggplot(data = <DATA>) +
  <GEOM_FUNCTION>(
    mapping = aes(<MAPPINGS>),
    stat = <STAT>,
    position = <POSITION>
  ) +
  <COORDINATE_FUNCTION> +
  <FACET_FUNCTION> +
  <SCALE_FUNCTION> +
  <THEME_FUNCTION>


ggplot(data, aes(x, y))

Begin a plot that you finish by adding layers (geoms) with +.

last_plot()

Returns the last plot that was displayed.

ggsave("plot.png", width = 5, height = 5)

Saves the last plot as a 5”×5” file. File type is inferred from the extension.




Common aesthetic (aes) values







Aesthetic
Values




color / fill
a string, e.g. "red", "#RRGGBB"


linetype
integer or name: 0=“blank”, 1=“solid”, 2=“dashed”, 3=“dotted”, 4=“dotdash”, 5=“longdash”, 6=“twodash”


size
integer, in mm (point/text size)


linewidth
integer, in mm (line width)


shape
integer 0–25, a shape name, or a single character, e.g. "a"

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Geoms
A geom function represents your data as a visual layer. Its aesthetic arguments map variables to visual properties like position, size, and color.

One variable
Continuous: geom_area(stat = "bin"), geom_density(kernel = "gaussian"), geom_dotplot(), geom_freqpoly(), geom_histogram(binwidth = 5), geom_qq(aes(sample = x))
Discrete: geom_bar()


Two variables
Both continuous: geom_label(), geom_point(), geom_quantile(), geom_rug(), geom_smooth(method = lm), geom_text()
One discrete, one continuous: geom_col(), geom_boxplot(), geom_dotplot(), geom_violin()
Both discrete: geom_count(), geom_jitter()


Continuous bivariate distribution & continuous function
geom_bin2d(binwidth = c(0.25,500)) geom_density_2d() geom_hex() geom_area() geom_line() geom_step(direction = "hv")


Visualizing error & maps
geom_crossbar() geom_errorbar() / geom_errorbarh() geom_linerange() geom_pointrange() geom_sf(aes(fill = ...))
For maps, read spatial data with sf (e.g. sf::st_read(...)) and draw it with geom_sf().


Three variables
geom_contour(aes(z = z)) geom_contour_filled(aes(fill = z)) geom_raster(aes(fill = z)) geom_tile(aes(fill = z))


Graphical primitives & line segments
geom_blank() geom_curve() geom_path() geom_polygon() geom_rect() geom_ribbon() geom_abline() geom_hline() geom_vline() geom_segment() geom_spoke()

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Stats
A stat is an alternative way to build a layer: it builds new variables to plot (e.g. count, proportion) before a geom draws them. Every geom has a default stat, and every stat has a default geom — you can override either one.
# Equivalent ways to draw a bar chart of counts
ggplot(df, aes(x)) + geom_bar()
ggplot(df, aes(x)) + geom_bar(stat = "count")
ggplot(df, aes(x)) + stat_count(geom = "bar")
stat_bin() stat_count() stat_density() stat_bin_2d() stat_bin_hex() stat_contour() stat_summary() stat_summary_2d() stat_ecdf() stat_quantile() stat_smooth() stat_ellipse() stat_function() stat_qq() stat_unique()

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Scales
Scales map data values to the visual values of an aesthetic. Override a default with scale_<aesthetic>_<type>(), e.g. scale_fill_manual().
n <- d + geom_bar(aes(fill = fl))
n + scale_fill_manual(
  values = c("skyblue", "royalblue", "blue", "navy"),
  limits = c("d", "e", "p", "r"),
  breaks = c("d", "e", "p", "r"),
  name = "fuel", labels = c("D", "E", "P", "R")
)







Purpose
Functions




General purpose
scale_*_continuous(), scale_*_discrete(), scale_*_binned(), scale_*_identity(), scale_*_manual(values = c()), scale_*_date(), scale_*_datetime()


X & Y location
scale_x_log10(), scale_x_reverse(), scale_x_sqrt() (and y equivalents)


Color/fill — discrete
scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues"), scale_fill_grey()


Color/fill — continuous
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues"), scale_fill_gradient(low, high), scale_fill_gradient2(low, mid, high), scale_fill_gradientn(colors = ...)


Shape & size
scale_shape(), scale_shape_manual(values = c()), scale_size(), scale_radius(range = c()), scale_size_area(max_size = ...)

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Coordinate systems


coord_cartesian(xlim, ylim)

The default cartesian coordinate system, with optional axis limits.

coord_fixed(ratio = 1/2)

Cartesian coordinates with a fixed aspect ratio between x and y units.

coord_flip()

Flip cartesian coordinates by switching the x and y aesthetic mappings.

coord_polar(theta = "x")

Polar coordinates.

coord_trans(y = "sqrt")

Transformed cartesian coordinates.

coord_sf()

Ensures all layers share a common Coordinate Reference System — use with geom_sf().

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Position adjustments
Position adjustments determine how geoms that would otherwise overlap get arranged.


position = "dodge"

Arrange elements side by side.

position = "fill"

Stack elements and normalize height to 100%.

position = "jitter"

Add random noise to x/y position to reduce overplotting.

position = "nudge"

Nudge labels away from their points.

position = "stack"

Stack elements on top of one another.



Recast a position as a function to pass extra arguments, e.g. s + geom_bar(position = position_dodge(width = 1)).

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Faceting
Facets divide a plot into subplots based on the values of one or more discrete variables.


facet_grid(. ~ fl)

Facet into columns based on fl.

facet_grid(year ~ .)

Facet into rows based on year.

facet_grid(year ~ fl)

Facet into both rows and columns.

facet_wrap(~ fl)

Wrap facets into a rectangular layout.



Let axis limits vary across facets with scales = "free" (or "free_x" / "free_y"), and relabel facet strips with labeller = label_both or label_bquote(...).

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Labels and legends
t + labs(
  x = "New x axis label",
  y = "New y axis label",
  title = "Add a title above the plot",
  subtitle = "Add a subtitle below title",
  caption = "Add a caption below plot",
  alt = "Add alt text to the plot"
)

t + annotate(geom = "text", x = 8, y = 9, label = "A")

p + guides(x = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2))   # avoid crowded axis labels
n + guides(fill = "none")                 # hide a legend
n + theme(legend.position = "bottom")     # place a legend
n + scale_fill_discrete(name = "Title", labels = c("A","B","C","D","E"))

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Themes
theme_bw() theme_gray() (default) theme_dark() theme_classic() theme_light() theme_linedraw() theme_minimal() theme_void()
Customize any theme element — axis, legend, panel, or facet properties — with theme():
u + theme(plot.title = element_text(...))
u + theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "blue"))

title: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Zooming


coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(10, 20))

Preferred. Zooms the view without clipping — data outside the range is still used for stats like smoothing.

xlim(0, 100) + ylim(10, 20)

Zooms with clipping — removes data outside the range before any stats are computed. Same effect as setting limits on scale_x_continuous() / scale_y_continuous().

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text: The stringr package provides an internally consistent set of tools for working with character strings — sequences of characters surrounded by quotation marks.

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Detect matches


str_detect(string, pattern)

Detect the presence of a pattern match. Also str_like() / str_ilike() for SQL LIKE/ILIKE-style wildcard matching. str_detect(fruit, "a")

str_starts(string, pattern)

Detect a match at the beginning of a string. Also str_ends(). str_starts(fruit, "a")

str_which(string, pattern)

Find the indexes of strings that contain a match. str_which(fruit, "a")

str_locate(string, pattern)

Locate the start/end position of a match. Also str_locate_all(). str_locate(fruit, "a")

str_count(string, pattern)

Count the number of matches in each string. str_count(fruit, "a")

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Subset strings


str_sub(string, start = 1L, end = -1L)

Extract substrings by position. str_sub(fruit, 1, 3); str_sub(fruit, -2)

str_subset(string, pattern)

Return only the strings that contain a match. str_subset(fruit, "p")

str_extract(string, pattern)

Return the first match found in each string. Also str_extract_all() for every match. str_extract(fruit, "[aeiou]")

str_match(string, pattern)

Return the first match as a matrix, with a column per () group in the pattern. Also str_match_all(). str_match(sentences, "(a|the) ([^ ]+)")

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Manage lengths


str_length(string)

The width of strings — the number of code points (usually characters).

str_pad(string, width, side)

Pad strings to a constant width. side can be “left”, “right”, or “both”.

str_trunc(string, width, side, ellipsis = "...")

Truncate strings, replacing cut content with an ellipsis.

str_trim(string, side)

Trim whitespace from the start and/or end.

str_squish(string)

Trim whitespace from both ends and collapse internal runs of spaces into one.

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Mutate strings


str_sub(string, s, e) <- value

Replace substrings identified with str_sub() by assigning into it. str_sub(fruit, 1, 3) <- "str"

str_replace(string, pattern, replacement)

Replace the first match in each string. Also str_remove(). str_replace(fruit, "p", "-")

str_replace_all(string, pattern, replacement)

Replace all matches. Also str_remove_all(). str_replace_all(fruit, "p", "-")

str_to_lower() / str_to_upper()

Convert case. locale defaults to "en".

str_to_title() / str_to_sentence()

Convert to title case or sentence case.

str_to_camel() / str_to_snake() / str_to_kebab()

Convert strings between programming case styles. str_to_camel("convert this string")

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Join and split


str_c(..., sep = "")

Join multiple strings into a single string. Also str_flatten() to collapse a vector into one string with a separator. str_c(letters, LETTERS)

str_dup(string, times)

Repeat strings a number of times. Also str_unique() to remove duplicates.

str_split_fixed(string, pattern, n)

Split into a matrix of substrings. Also str_split() (list output) and str_split_i() (ith substring).

str_glue(..., .envir = parent.frame())

Build a string from text and {expressions} to evaluate. Also str_glue_data() for a data frame/list/environment source. str_glue("Pi is {pi}")

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Order and helper functions


str_order(x) / str_sort(x)

Return sort indexes, or sort a character vector directly. Support numeric = TRUE for natural sort order.

str_view(string, pattern)

View an HTML rendering of every regex match — invaluable while developing a pattern.

str_equal(x, y, ignore_case = FALSE)

Determine whether two strings are equivalent.

str_wrap(string, width = 80)

Wrap strings into nicely formatted paragraphs.

str_conv(string, encoding)

Override the encoding of a string.

title: String Manipulation with stringr
text:
Regular expressions primer
Regular expressions (regexps) are a concise language for describing patterns in strings. Pattern arguments in stringr are interpreted as regex after R has parsed any special characters in the string itself — so a literal backslash in a pattern must be written as \\ in R code. Use writeLines() to see how R interprets a string after special characters are parsed.

Match characters







Write this
Means




\.
literal .


\d
any digit (\D for non-digits)


\s
any whitespace (\S for non-whitespace)


\w
any word character (\W for non-word)


\b
word boundary


[:digit:], [:alpha:], [:lower:], [:upper:]
character classes — digits, letters, lowercase, uppercase


[:alnum:], [:punct:], [:space:]
alphanumerics, punctuation, whitespace


.
any character except a newline





Quantifiers, anchors & alternation







Pattern
Matches




a?
zero or one


a*
zero or more


a+
one or more


a{n} / a{n,} / a{n,m}
exactly n / n or more / between n and m


^a
start of string


a$
end of string


ab\|d
“ab” or “d”


[abe] / [^abe]
one of / anything but


[a-c]
a range


(ab\|d)e
parentheses set precedence and create a group





Groups and lookarounds



Pattern
Matches




\1
refers back to the first () group


a(?=c)
“a” followed by “c” (not consumed)


a(?!c)
“a” not followed by “c”


(?<=b)a
“a” preceded by “b”


(?<!b)a
“a” not preceded by “b”





Pattern interpretation modifiers


regex(pattern, ignore_case = FALSE, multiline = FALSE, dotall = FALSE)

Modify how a pattern is interpreted — case-insensitivity, multi-line anchors, comments, or . matching newlines.

fixed()

Match raw bytes (fast), but may miss characters representable in multiple encodings.

coll()

Match using locale-specific collation rules (slower, more correct for non-ASCII text).

boundary()

Match boundaries between characters, line breaks, sentences, or words. str_split(sentences, boundary("word"))









Tip



Not sure what a pattern actually matches? Run it through str_view() first — it highlights every match inline, which is much faster than guessing.

title: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time
text: This site collects the essentials from Posit’s official cheatsheets into a single, browsable reference — from finding your way around the RStudio IDE to importing, wrangling, and visualizing data with the tidyverse.
crumbs: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time

title: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time
text:
Topics



🖥️ RStudio IDE


Panes, source editor, projects, version control, debugging, and keyboard shortcuts.

 

📥 Importing Data


Read delimited files, Excel workbooks, and Google Sheets with readr, readxl, and googlesheets4.

 

🔧 Transforming Data


Filter, arrange, mutate, summarize, group, and join data frames with dplyr.

 

🔤 Strings


Detect, extract, replace, and format text with stringr, plus a regular expressions primer.

 

🏷️ Factors


Create, reorder, recode, and combine categorical variables with forcats.

 

📊 Data Visualization


Build plots layer by layer — geoms, stats, scales, facets, and themes — with ggplot2.
crumbs: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time

title: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time
text:
Why the tidyverse?
Every reference on this site centers on the tidyverse, a collection of R packages designed to work together around a shared philosophy: data should be tidy — each variable in its own column, each observation in its own row — and functions should be predictable, pipeable, and human-readable.

readr — import dplyr — transform stringr — text forcats — factors ggplot2 — visualize RStudio — workbench
crumbs: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time

title: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time
text:
A typical R workflow

Set up your project. Open RStudio, create a Project (File > New Project), and organize your scripts, data, and outputs. See RStudio IDE.
Import your data. Read CSVs, Excel files, or Google Sheets into tibbles with read_csv(), read_excel(), or read_sheet(). See Importing Data.
Clean and reshape it. Filter rows, select columns, create new variables, and summarize groups with dplyr verbs. See Transforming Data.
Wrangle text and categories. Clean up messy text with stringr and tame categorical variables with forcats. See Strings and Factors.
Visualize and share. Build layered plots with ggplot2, then knit results into a report with R Markdown or Quarto. See Data Visualization.
crumbs: Learn RStudio and R, one cheatsheet at a time

title: Importing Data
text: One of the first steps in any project is getting outside data into R. The tidyverse provides readr for delimited text files, readxl for Excel workbooks, and googlesheets4 for Google Sheets.

title: Importing Data
text:
Reading tabular data with readr
read_*(file, col_names = TRUE, col_types = NULL, col_select = NULL, id = NULL,
       locale, n_max = Inf, skip = 0, na = c("", "NA"),
       guess_max = min(1000, n_max), show_col_types = TRUE)


read_csv("file.csv")

Read a comma-delimited file with period decimal marks.

read_csv2("file2.csv")

Read semicolon-delimited files with comma decimal marks (common in European locales).

read_tsv("file.tsv")

Read a tab-delimited file. Also read_table() for whitespace-separated files.

read_delim("file.txt", delim = "|")

Read files with any delimiter. If none is specified, readr guesses it automatically.

read_fwf("file.tsv", fwf_widths(c(2, 2, NA)))

Read a fixed-width file by specifying each column’s width.




Useful read arguments







Goal
Code




No header row
read_csv("file.csv", col_names = FALSE)


Provide your own header
read_csv("file.csv", col_names = c("x", "y", "z"))


Read multiple files into one table
read_csv(c("f1.csv","f2.csv","f3.csv"), id = "origin_file")


Skip lines
read_csv("file.csv", skip = 1)


Read only a subset of lines
read_csv("file.csv", n_max = 1)


Treat a value as missing
read_csv("file.csv", na = c("1"))


Specify decimal marks
read_delim("file2.csv", locale = locale(decimal_mark = ","))


Hide the column-spec message
read_*(file, show_col_types = FALSE)


Select columns to import
read_*(file, col_select = c(age, earn))


Guess column types from more rows
read_*(file, guess_max = Inf) — by default readr looks at the first 1000 rows.

title: Importing Data
text:
Column specification
Column specifications define what data type each column will be imported as. By default, readr generates and prints a spec summary when a file is read; inspect it any time with spec(x).



Function
Abbreviation




col_logical()
"l"


col_integer()
"i"


col_double()
"d"


col_number()
"n"


col_character()
"c"


col_factor(levels, ordered = FALSE)
"f"


col_datetime(format = "")
"T"


col_date(format = "")
"D"


col_time(format = "")
"t"


col_skip()
"-" / "_"


col_guess()
"?"



# Set a default type for all columns
read_csv(file, col_type = list(.default = col_double()))

# Mix column type functions and string abbreviations
read_csv(file, col_type = list(x = col_double(), y = "l", z = "_"))

# Or a single compact string of abbreviations
read_csv(file, col_type = "_?ilc")

title: Importing Data
text:
Saving data with readr


write_csv(x, file)

Write a comma-delimited file.

write_csv2(x, file)

Write a semicolon-delimited file.

write_tsv(x, file)

Write a tab-delimited file.

write_delim(x, file, delim = " ")

Write with any delimiter you choose.

title: Importing Data
text:
Other data sources
haven — SPSS / Stata / SAS · DBI — databases · jsonlite — JSON · xml2 — XML · httr — web APIs · rvest — HTML / web scraping · readr::read_lines() — raw text

title: Importing Data
text:
Importing spreadsheets

Excel files with readxl


read_excel("excel_file.xlsx")

Read a .xls or .xlsx file based on its extension. Also read_xls() and read_xlsx() to force a format.

read_excel(path, sheet = 1)

Choose a sheet by position or name: read_excel(path, sheet = "s1").

excel_sheets(path)

Get a vector of sheet names — useful before reading multiple sheets in a loop.

read_excel(path, range = "Sheet1!B1:D2")

Read a subset of cells. Also see cell_limits(), cell_rows(), cell_cols(), and anchored().



To read every sheet in a workbook into one combined data frame:
path <- "your_file_path.xlsx"
path |>
  excel_sheets() |>
  set_names() |>
  map(read_excel, path = path) |>
  list_rbind()
Column types: set every column at once (col_types = "text") or individually (col_types = c("text", "guess", "guess", "numeric")). Guess more rows with guess_max = Inf. For writing Excel files, see openxlsx or writexl; for non-tabular Excel content, see tidyxl.


Google Sheets with googlesheets4


read_sheet(ss, sheet = NULL, range = NULL)

Read a sheet from a URL, a Sheet ID, or a dribble from googledrive. Same as range_read().

gs4_get(ss) / sheet_properties(ss)

Get spreadsheet metadata or a tibble of properties for each worksheet. Also sheet_names() and gs4_find(...).

write_sheet(data, ss, sheet)

Write a data frame into a new or existing sheet.

gs4_create(name, ..., sheets = NULL)

Create a brand-new Sheet from a vector of names, a data frame, or a named list of data frames.

sheet_append(ss, data, sheet = 1)

Add rows to the end of an existing worksheet.



Sheets URLs follow the pattern https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/SPREADSHEET_ID/edit#gid=SHEET_ID. For whole-file operations (renaming, sharing, moving between folders), use the companion package googledrive.






Note



Both readxl and googlesheets4 support the same col_types abbreviations as readr ("l", "i", "d", "n", "c", "D", "T", "?", "_"), plus "L" for list-columns when a column mixes multiple data types.

title: RStudio IDE
text: RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for R. It wraps the R console in four main panes — Source, Console, Environment/History, and Files/Plots/Packages/Help — plus tools for projects, version control, package development, and debugging.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
The four panes
By default RStudio arranges its panes in a 2×2 grid. Drag pane boundaries to resize, or use the maximize/minimize icons on each pane’s toolbar.


Source Editor

Where you write and edit scripts (.R), R Markdown/Quarto documents, Shiny apps, and more. Includes syntax highlighting, tab completion, code diagnostics, multi-cursor editing (Alt/Option + drag), and a file outline for jumping to functions or sections.

Console / Terminal / Jobs

Run R code interactively in the Console, use the Terminal tab for shell commands, and run long scripts in the background with Jobs so your console stays free.

Environment / History / Connections

Environment lists your saved objects by type, with tools to load/save the workspace and clear it. History shows past commands you can re-run or copy. Connections manages external databases.

Files / Plots / Packages / Help / Viewer

Files is a browser keyed to your working directory. Plots shows a history of your graphics. Packages lists and manages installed packages. Help displays documentation. Viewer renders HTML content like Shiny apps and R Markdown/Quarto output.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Documents and apps
RStudio recognizes file types and opens them with the right tools automatically.







File / project type
What RStudio gives you




R scripts (.R)
Run selected code, re-run previous code, source with/without echo, or as a local job.


R Markdown / Quarto (.Rmd, .qmd)
Knit/render button, chunk execution controls, spell check, and a Visual Editor for WYSIWYG markdown editing.


Shiny apps (app.R, or ui.R + server.R + global.R)
A Run App button, a chooser for where to view the app (window, viewer pane, or browser), and one-click publishing to shinyapps.io or Posit Connect.


R packages
A Build pane with Install & Restart, devtools::load_all(), R CMD check, and package tests, plus Roxygen-based documentation.









Tip



The Visual Editor for R Markdown/Quarto behaves like a word processor: format text, insert tables, citations, and equations, and it stays in sync with the underlying markdown source.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Projects
Create a project with File > New Project. RStudio saves the call history, workspace, and working directory associated with a project and reloads them each time you reopen it — this keeps unrelated analyses cleanly separated. Projects can also be shared with collaborators, run in multiple simultaneous R sessions, and switched between different R versions.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Version control (Git)
Turn on Git integration at Tools > Project Options > Git/SVN. The Git pane shows file status at a glance and lets you stage, commit, and push/pull without leaving RStudio.



Status letter
Meaning




A
Added


D
Deleted


M
Modified


R
Renamed


?
Untracked



Stage files, commit with a message, view file diffs, browse commit history, and push/pull to a remote — all from the Git pane toolbar. An embedded shell is also available for anything not covered by the GUI.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Package development
Start a new package with File > New Project > New Directory > R Package, then enable Roxygen documentation at Tools > Project Options > Build Tools. The Build pane gives you:


devtools::load_all()

Reload the package’s changed code without a full install — the fastest development loop.

Install and Restart

Install the package and restart R with it freshly loaded.

Run R CMD check

Run the standard CRAN-style package checks for structural and documentation issues.

Run package tests

Execute your test suite (e.g. testthat) from the Build pane.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Debug mode
Trigger the debugger with debug(), browser(), or by clicking next to a line number to set a breakpoint, then execute your code. While paused, RStudio highlights the current line and gives you:

Step controls — step through code one line at a time, or step into/out of functions.
Environment inspection — examine variables in the currently executing environment.
Console access — run commands directly in the paused environment.
Traceback — open the traceback to see the sequence of function calls that led to an error, and jump the debugger to its origin.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Posit Assistant
Posit Assistant is a built-in data analysis assistant that connects to your live R and Python sessions. It can see your data and help you explore, visualize, build, and debug — with a mode selector (Normal, Plan, Auto, Cleaning), slash commands, web search, and the ability to reference workspace files with @.

title: RStudio IDE
text:
Essential keyboard shortcuts



Action
Windows / Linux
Mac




Search command history
Ctrl + ↑
Cmd + ↑


Interrupt current command
Esc
Esc


Clear console
Ctrl + L
Ctrl + L


Go to File/Function
Ctrl + .
Ctrl + .


Attempt completion
Tab / Ctrl+Space
Tab / Ctrl+Space


Insert <-
Alt + -
Option + -


Insert \|> pipe
Ctrl+Shift+M
Cmd+Shift+M


(Un)Comment selection
Ctrl+Shift+C
Cmd+Shift+C


Knit/Render document
Ctrl+Shift+K
Cmd+Shift+K


Load all (devtools)
Ctrl+Shift+L
Cmd+Shift+L


Test package

title: Factors with forcats
text: R represents categorical data with factors. A factor is an integer vector with a levels attribute that maps integers to categorical values — when you view a factor, R displays the levels, not the underlying integers. The forcats package provides tools for working with them.

title: Factors with forcats
text:
Creating and inspecting factors


factor(x, levels, labels = levels, ordered = FALSE)

Convert a vector to a factor. Also as_factor(). f <- factor(c("a","c","b","a"), levels = c("a","b","c"))

levels(x)

Return or set the levels of a factor. levels(f); levels(f) <- c("x","y","z")









Note



Use unclass() on a factor to see its underlying integer/levels structure.



Inspect factors


fct_count(f, sort = FALSE, prop = FALSE)

Count the number of values with each level.

fct_match(f, lvls)

Check whether given levels are present in f.

fct_unique(f)

Return the unique values, removing duplicates.

title: Factors with forcats
text:
Change the order of levels


fct_relevel(.f, ..., after = 0L)

Manually reorder factor levels. fct_relevel(f, c("b", "c", "a"))

fct_infreq(f)

Reorder levels by frequency of appearance, highest first. Also fct_inseq().

fct_inorder(f)

Reorder levels by the order in which they first appear in the data.

fct_rev(f)

Reverse level order.

fct_shift(f)

Shift levels left or right, wrapping around the end.

fct_shuffle(f)

Randomly permute the order of factor levels.

fct_reorder(.f, .x, .fun = median)

Reorder levels by their relationship with another variable — great for ordered bar/box plots. boxplot(weight ~ fct_reorder(group, weight), data = PlantGrowth)

fct_reorder2(.f, .x, .y, .fun = last2)

Reorder levels by their final values when plotted against two other variables — handy for coloring line plots so the legend order matches the lines.

title: Factors with forcats
text:
Change the value of levels


fct_recode(.f, ...)

Manually rename levels. Also fct_relabel(), which applies a function (purrr-style) to each level. fct_recode(f, v = "a", x = "b", z = "c")

fct_anon(f, prefix = "")

Anonymize levels by replacing them with random integers.

fct_collapse(.f, ..., other_level = NULL)

Collapse levels into manually defined groups. fct_collapse(f, x = c("a", "b"))

fct_lump_min(f, min)

Lump together levels that appear fewer than min times into “Other”. Also fct_lump_n(), fct_lump_prop(), fct_lump_lowfreq().

fct_other(f, keep, drop, other_level = "Other")

Replace levels not in keep (or in drop) with “Other”.

title: Factors with forcats
text:
Add or drop levels


fct_drop(f, only)

Drop unused levels.

fct_expand(f, ...)

Add new levels to a factor. fct_expand(f, "x")

fct_na_value_to_level(f, level = "(Missing)")

Assign an explicit level to NAs so they show up in plots and tables.

title: Factors with forcats
text:
Combine factors


fct_c(...)

Combine factors that have different levels. Also fct_cross(). fct_c(f1, f2)

fct_unify(fs, levels = lvls_union(fs))

Standardize levels across a list of factors so they can be safely combined or compared.









Tip



A quick mental model: creating and reordering levels changes how a factor displays and sorts (great for plots and tables); recoding, collapsing, and lumping change what the levels actually mean.

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text: dplyr functions work with pipes and expect tidy data: each variable in its own column, each observation (case) in its own row. x |> f(y) becomes f(x, y).

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Extract cases (rows)
Row functions return a subset of rows as a new table.


filter(.data, ...)

Extract rows that meet logical criteria. mtcars |> filter(mpg > 20)

filter_out(.data, ...)

Drop rows that meet logical criteria — the complement of filter(). Missing values in the dropped condition are kept by default. mtcars |> filter_out(mpg > 20)

when_any() / when_all()

Use inside filter() to combine multiple conditions. mtcars |> filter(when_any(mpg > 30, hp > 300))

distinct(.data, ...)

Remove rows with duplicate values. mtcars |> distinct(gear)

slice(.data, ...)

Select rows by position. mtcars |> slice(10:15)

slice_sample(.data, n, prop, replace)

Randomly select rows, by count or fraction. mtcars |> slice_sample(n = 5, replace = TRUE)

slice_min() / slice_max()

Select rows with the lowest/highest values of a variable. mtcars |> slice_min(mpg, prop = 0.25)

slice_head() / slice_tail()

Select the first or last rows. mtcars |> slice_head(n = 5)




Logical & comparison operators for filter()
== != < > <= >= is.na() !is.na() %in% ! | & xor()


Arrange & add cases


arrange(.data, ...)

Order rows by column values, low to high. Use desc() for high to low. mtcars |> arrange(desc(mpg))

add_row(.data, ...)

Add one or more rows to a table. cars |> add_row(speed = 1, dist = 1)

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Manipulate variables (columns)


pull(.data, var = -1)

Extract column values as a vector, by name or index. mtcars |> pull(wt)

select(.data, ...)

Extract columns as a table. mtcars |> select(mpg, wt)

relocate(.data, ...)

Move columns to a new position. mtcars |> relocate(mpg, cyl, .after = last_col())

mutate(.data, ...)

Compute new column(s) with vectorized functions. Also add_column(). mtcars |> mutate(gpm = 1 / mpg)

rename(.data, ...)

Rename columns. Use rename_with() to rename with a function. mtcars |> rename(miles_per_gallon = mpg)




Selection helpers
Use with select() and across(), e.g. mtcars |> select(mpg:cyl):
contains(match) starts_with(match) ends_with(match) matches(match) num_range(prefix, range) all_of(x) / any_of(x) : (e.g. mpg:cyl) ! (e.g. !gear) everything()


Apply a function across multiple columns


across(.cols, .funs, ...)

Summarize or mutate multiple columns the same way. df |> summarize(across(everything(), mean))

c_across(.cols)

Compute across columns in row-wise data. df |> rowwise() |> mutate(x_total = sum(c_across(1:2)))

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Group and summarize cases


group_by(.data, ...)

Create a “grouped” copy of a table. Subsequent dplyr verbs operate on each group separately, then combine the results. mtcars |> group_by(cyl) |> summarize(avg = mean(mpg))

.by = argument

Alternate grouping syntax, scoped to a single call. mtcars |> summarize(avg = mean(mpg), .by = cyl)

summarize(.data, ...)

Compute a table of summary statistics — summary functions take a vector and return one value. mtcars |> summarize(avg = mean(mpg))

count(.data, ..., sort = FALSE)

Count rows in each group. Also tally(), add_count(), add_tally(). mtcars |> count(cyl)

rowwise(.data, ...)

Group data into individual rows so dplyr computes per-row (useful with list-columns). starwars |> rowwise() |> mutate(film_count = length(films))

ungroup(x, ...)

Return an ungrouped copy of a table. ungroup(g_mtcars)

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Vectorized functions (for mutate)
Vectorized functions take a vector as input and return a vector of the same length as output.







Category
Functions




Offset
lag(), lead()


Cumulative
cumall(), cumany(), cummax(), cummean(), cummin(), cumprod(), cumsum()


Ranking
cume_dist(), dense_rank(), min_rank(), ntile(), percent_rank(), row_number()


Math
+ - * / ^ %/% %%, log(), log2(), log10(), between(), near()


Conditional / recode
if_else(), na_if(), case_when(), replace_when(), coalesce(), recode_values(), replace_values()


Element-wise extremes
pmax(), pmin()



starwars |>
  mutate(type = case_when(
    height > 200 | mass > 200 ~ "large",
    species == "Droid" ~ "robot",
    .default = "other"
  ))

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Summary functions (for summarize)
Summary functions take a vector as input and return a single value.



Category
Functions




Count
n(), n_distinct(), sum(!is.na())


Position
mean(), median()


Logical
mean() (proportion TRUE), sum() (count TRUE)


Order
first(), last(), nth()


Rank
quantile(), min(), max()


Spread
IQR(), mad(), sd(), var()

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Combine tables

Stack rows or columns


bind_rows(..., .id = NULL)

Stack tables on top of each other. Set .id to add a column identifying the source table.

bind_cols(...)

Place tables side by side. Column counts must match — rows are not matched by key.





Mutating joins
Join one table to columns from another, matching rows by key.







Function
Keeps




left_join(x, y, by = ...)
All rows of x, matched values from y.


right_join(x, y, by = ...)
All rows of y, matched values from x.


inner_join(x, y, by = ...)
Only rows with matches in both tables.


full_join(x, y, by = ...)
All rows from both tables.



# Match on a shared column name
left_join(x, y, by = "A")

# Match on columns with different names in each table
left_join(x, y, by = c("C" = "D"))

# Add suffixes to disambiguate same-named unmatched columns
left_join(x, y, by = c("C" = "D"), suffix = c("1", "2"))


Filtering & nest joins


semi_join(x, y, by = ...)

Return rows of x that have a match in y — useful for previewing a join.

anti_join(x, y, by = ...)

Return rows of x that have no match in y.

nest_join(x, y, by = ...)

Inner join y into x as a nested data-frame column.





Set operations


intersect(x, y)

Rows that appear in both x and y.

setdiff(x, y)

Rows that appear in x but not y.

union(x, y)

Rows in x or y, duplicates removed. union_all() keeps duplicates.









Tip



Use setequal(x, y) to test whether two data sets contain exactly the same rows, in any order.

title: Transforming Data with dplyr
text:
Row names
Tidy data doesn’t use row names — move them into a real column instead:
mtcars |> tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "car")
a |> tibble::column_to_rownames(var = "car")
